"The article critiques the 오래standing “great man” theory of history, which claims that exceptional individuals — usually powerful, charismatic, and supposedly heroic men — are the main drivers of historical change. It traces this idea back to 19th-century thinker Thomas Carlyle, who celebrated figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and Muhammad as towering personalities who shaped the world through force of will and genius, while ordinary people merely observed and followed. The piece argues that this view remains seductive even though modern egalitarian thought, Marxist analysis, and the “history from below” approach have challenged it for decades. 

But the article’s central point is that in the modern era, people who imagine themselves as such heroic figures are often not heroes at all. Instead, they are more accurately understood as anti-heroes or outright villains. These are men who believe they have a special destiny, mission, or sacred duty to lead others, and who are convinced they alone possess the insight needed to govern. Because they see themselves as uniquely capable and morally justified, they can become ruthless, arrogant, and willing to impose their vision on others without restraint. 

The opening suggests a broader warning: although the “great man” myth is historically influential, it is dangerous when adopted by contemporary political and social leaders who use claims of greatness to excuse domination, coercion, or destructive behavior. In other words, the article challenges the romance of heroic leadership and implies that modern history is often shaped not by noble saviors, but by self-regarding strongmen whose power makes them far more threatening than admirable."
